newsitem.title: UK: Cash flow strength to fund airlines' fleet renewal.
newsitem.headline: Cash flow strength to fund airlines' fleet renewal.

text.p: Airlines are producing the kind of cash-flow which could generate around $50 billion over the three years 1995-1997 and can afford some renewal of their fleets, International Air Transport Association (IATA) director-general Pierre Jeanniot said on Monday.

"That is, perhaps $15 or $16 billion in profit after interest during the three years and perhaps $35 to $40 billion in depreciation," he said in a speech prepared for delivery at a conference on the future of air transport.

"If they raise another $50 billion on the financial market, and if we assume that on average planes cost about $70 to 80 million each, allowing for a small/medium/big mix, then they could acquire some 1,200 to 1,400 aircraft without deteriorating their balance sheets from their current debt/equity levels," he added.
This renewal is necessary if aircraft are to meet agreed standards for quieter planes by the year 2000, he said.
Jeanniot added that while most airlines are profitable, only about a third of them are earning net profits at or above the four percent level.
In 1995 IATA members recorded a net profit of $5.2 billion on revenues of $128.8 billion, an all-time record in dollar terms.
"This year should certainly deliver another profit but it will be lower than 1995," he said.

On fuel costs, he added that recent action (to raise passenger fares and introduce cargo surcharges) was prompted in part," by the September cruise missile action in the Gulf which we calculate cost the IATA carriers an additional $832 million in extra fuel costs alone." --Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax +44 171 542 5017
